```sql
WITH customer_date_range AS (
  SELECT 
    customer_id,
    MIN(txn_date) AS min_date,
    MAX(txn_date) AS max_date
  FROM customer_transactions
  GROUP BY customer_id
),

all_dates AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT txn_date FROM customer_transactions
),

calendar AS (
  SELECT 
    customer_id,
    txn_date
  FROM customer_date_range
  JOIN all_dates ON txn_date BETWEEN min_date AND max_date
),

txn_per_day AS (
  SELECT 
    customer_id,
    txn_date,
    COALESCE(SUM(txn_amount), 0) AS daily_amount
  FROM customer_transactions
  GROUP BY customer_id, txn_date
),

balances_unadjusted AS (
  SELECT 
    c.customer_id, c.txn_date,
    COALESCE(t.daily_amount, 0) AS daily_amount
  FROM calendar c
  LEFT JOIN txn_per_day t ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id AND c.txn_date = t.txn_date
  ORDER BY c.customer_id, c.txn_date
),

balances_with_carryforward AS (
  SELECT 
    customer_id, txn_date,
    MAX(
      SUM(daily_amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY txn_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
    , 0) AS daily_balance
  FROM balances_unadjusted
),

monthly_max_balances AS (
  SELECT 
    customer_id,
    STRFTIME('%Y-%m', txn_date) AS year_month,
    MAX(daily_balance) AS max_daily_balance
  FROM balances_with_carryforward
  GROUP BY customer_id, year_month
),

monthly_total AS (
  SELECT 
    year_month,
    SUM(max_daily_balance) AS total_monthly_max_balance
  FROM monthly_max_balances
  GROUP BY year_month
)

SELECT * FROM monthly_total
ORDER BY year_month;
```

```sql
    FROM customers c
    JOIN invoices i ON c.CustomerId = i.CustomerId

sales_filtered AS (

median_calc AS (

           COUNT(*) OVER () AS total_count
    FROM sales_filtered
)
SELECT AVG(total_sales) AS median_sales
```

```sql
WITH monthly_inserts AS (
  SELECT
    STRFTIME('%Y', inserted_at) AS year,
    STRFTIME('%m', inserted_at) AS month,
    COUNT(*) AS cities_added
  FROM cities
  WHERE inserted_at >= '2021-04-01' AND inserted_at < '2023-07-01'
    AND month IN ('04', '05', '06')
  GROUP BY year, month
),
running_totals AS (
  SELECT
    year,
    month,
    cities_added,
    SUM(cities_added) OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY year ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
  FROM monthly_inserts
),
growth_calc AS (
  SELECT
    current.year,
    current.month,
    current.cities_added,
    current.running_total,

    -- Monthly YoY Growth %
    CASE 
      WHEN prev_year.cities_added IS NOT NULL THEN 
        ROUND(100.0 * (current.cities_added - prev_year.cities_added) / prev_year.cities_added, 2)
      ELSE NULL
    END AS monthly_yoy_growth_pct,

    -- Running Total YoY Growth %
    CASE
      WHEN prev_year.running_total IS NOT NULL THEN
        ROUND(100.0 * (current.running_total - prev_year.running_total) / prev_year.running_total, 2)
      ELSE NULL
    END AS running_total_yoy_growth_pct

  FROM running_totals current
  LEFT JOIN running_totals prev_year
    ON current.month = prev_year.month
   AND CAST(current.year AS INTEGER) = CAST(prev_year.year AS INTEGER) + 1
)
SELECT
  year,
  month,
  cities_added,
  running_total,
  monthly_yoy_growth_pct,
  running_total_yoy_growth_pct
FROM growth_calc
WHERE year IN ('2022', '2023')
ORDER BY month, year;
```

```sql
WITH
-- Calculate total runs per batsman per season
batsman_runs AS (
  SELECT
    m.season_id,
    p.player_id,
    SUM(bs.runs_scored) AS total_runs
  FROM batsman_scored bs
  JOIN player_match pm ON bs.match_id = pm.match_id AND bs.batsman_id = pm.player_id
  JOIN match m ON pm.match_id = m.match_id
  JOIN player p ON p.player_id = pm.player_id
  GROUP BY m.season_id, p.player_id
),
-- Rank batsmen by total_runs desc, player_id asc per season and pick top 3
top_batsmen AS (
  SELECT
    season_id,
    player_id,
    total_runs,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY season_id ORDER BY total_runs DESC, player_id ASC) AS rn
  FROM batsman_runs
  WHERE total_runs > 0
),
-- Filter top 3 batsmen per season
top3_batsmen AS (
  SELECT season_id, player_id, total_runs, rn
  FROM top_batsmen
  WHERE rn <= 3
),
-- Calculate total wickets per bowler per season excluding specified dismissal kinds
bowler_wickets AS (
  SELECT
    m.season_id,
    wt.player_id,
    COUNT(*) AS total_wickets
  FROM wicket_taken wt
  JOIN match m ON wt.match_id = m.match_id
  WHERE wt.dismissal_kind NOT IN ('run out', 'hit wicket', 'retired hurt')
  GROUP BY m.season_id, wt.player_id
),
-- Rank bowlers by total_wickets desc, player_id asc per season and pick top 3
top_bowlers AS (
  SELECT
    season_id,
    player_id,
    total_wickets,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY season_id ORDER BY total_wickets DESC, player_id ASC) AS rn
  FROM bowler_wickets
  WHERE total_wickets > 0
),
-- Filter top 3 bowlers per season
top3_bowlers AS (
  SELECT season_id, player_id, total_wickets, rn
  FROM top_bowlers
  WHERE rn <= 3
)
-- Final output joining top 3 batsmen and top 3 bowlers by same rank and season
SELECT

  b.rn AS position,
  b.player_id AS batsman_id,

FROM top3_batsmen b

ORDER BY b.season_id, b.rn;
```

```sql
WITH sales_us AS (
  SELECT cu.cust_city AS city, s.prod_id, t.calendar_year, t.calendar_quarter_number AS quarter, SUM(s.amount_sold) AS total_sales
  FROM sales s
  JOIN customers cu ON s.cust_id = cu.cust_id
  JOIN countries co ON cu.country_id = co.country_id
  JOIN times t ON s.time_id = t.time_id
  WHERE co.country_name = 'United States' 
    AND s.promo_id = 0
    AND ((t.calendar_year = 2019 AND t.calendar_quarter_number = 4) OR (t.calendar_year = 2020 AND t.calendar_quarter_number = 4))
  GROUP BY cu.cust_city, s.prod_id, t.calendar_year, t.calendar_quarter_number
),
city_sales AS (
  SELECT sales_us.city,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sales_us.calendar_year = 2019 THEN sales_us.total_sales ELSE 0 END) AS sales_2019,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sales_us.calendar_year = 2020 THEN sales_us.total_sales ELSE 0 END) AS sales_2020
  FROM sales_us
  GROUP BY sales_us.city
  HAVING sales_2020 >= sales_2019 * 1.2
),
filtered_products AS (
  SELECT su.city, su.prod_id,
    SUM(CASE WHEN su.calendar_year = 2019 THEN su.total_sales ELSE 0 END) AS sales_2019,
    SUM(CASE WHEN su.calendar_year = 2020 THEN su.total_sales ELSE 0 END) AS sales_2020
  FROM sales_us su
  JOIN city_sales cs ON su.city = cs.city
  GROUP BY su.city, su.prod_id
),
products_ranked AS (
  SELECT fp.city, fp.prod_id, fp.sales_2019, fp.sales_2020,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY fp.city ORDER BY (fp.sales_2019 + fp.sales_2020) DESC) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY fp.city) AS cnt
  FROM filtered_products fp
),
top_products AS (
  SELECT city, prod_id, sales_2019, sales_2020
  FROM products_ranked
  WHERE rn <= CEIL(cnt * 0.2)
),
city_totals AS (
  SELECT su.city,
    SUM(CASE WHEN su.calendar_year = 2019 THEN su.total_sales ELSE 0 END) AS total_2019,
    SUM(CASE WHEN su.calendar_year = 2020 THEN su.total_sales ELSE 0 END) AS total_2020
  FROM sales_us su
  JOIN city_sales cs ON su.city = cs.city
  GROUP BY su.city
),
product_shares AS (
  SELECT tp.city, tp.prod_id,
  tp.sales_2019 * 1.0 / ct.total_2019 AS share_2019,
  tp.sales_2020 * 1.0 / ct.total_2020 AS share_2020,
  tp.sales_2020 * 1.0 / ct.total_2020 - tp.sales_2019 * 1.0 / ct.total_2019 AS share_change
  FROM top_products tp
  JOIN city_totals ct ON tp.city = ct.city
)

SELECT city, prod_id AS product_id, share_2019, share_2020, share_change
FROM product_shares
ORDER BY share_change DESC
LIMIT 1000;
```

WITH OrderedCities AS (
  SELECT
    geolocation_state,
    geolocation_city,
    geolocation_zip_code_prefix,
    geolocation_lat,
    geolocation_lng,
    LAG(geolocation_lat) OVER (
      ORDER BY geolocation_state, geolocation_city, geolocation_zip_code_prefix, geolocation_lat, geolocation_lng
    ) AS prev_lat,
    LAG(geolocation_lng) OVER (
      ORDER BY geolocation_state, geolocation_city, geolocation_zip_code_prefix, geolocation_lat, geolocation_lng
    ) AS prev_lng,
    LAG(geolocation_city) OVER (
      ORDER BY geolocation_state, geolocation_city, geolocation_zip_code_prefix, geolocation_lat, geolocation_lng
    ) AS prev_city,
    LAG(geolocation_state) OVER (
      ORDER BY geolocation_state, geolocation_city, geolocation_zip_code_prefix, geolocation_lat, geolocation_lng
    ) AS prev_state
  FROM olist_geolocation
),
Distances AS (
  SELECT
    geolocation_state,
    geolocation_city,
    prev_state,
    prev_city,
    -- Convert degrees to radians: degrees * PI()/180
    6371 * ACOS(
      COS(RADIANS(prev_lat)) * COS(RADIANS(geolocation_lat)) * COS(RADIANS(geolocation_lng) - RADIANS(prev_lng))
      + SIN(RADIANS(prev_lat)) * SIN(RADIANS(geolocation_lat))
    ) AS distance_km
  FROM OrderedCities
  WHERE prev_lat IS NOT NULL AND prev_lng IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT
  prev_state AS state1,
  prev_city AS city1,
  geolocation_state AS state2,
  geolocation_city AS city2,
  distance_km
FROM Distances
ORDER BY distance_km DESC
LIMIT 1;

The distance between two cities can be calculated using the **Spherical Law of Cosines**. This method estimates the distance based on the geographical coordinates (latitude and longitude) of the cities. Below is a detailed explanation of the calculation process, including the relevant formula.

The distance $d$ between two cities is calculated using the following formula:

$$
d = 6371 \times \arccos \left( \cos(\text{lat}_1) \times \cos(\text{lat}_2) \times \cos(\text{lon}_2 - \text{lon}_1) + \sin(\text{lat}_1) \times \sin(\text{lat}_2) \right)
$$

- $\text{lon}_1$ and $\text{lon}_2$ are the longitudes of the first and second cities in **radians**.

```sql
WITH RankedDates AS (
  SELECT
    c.country_code_2 AS country_code,
    date(c.insert_date) AS inserted_city_date,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.country_code_2 ORDER BY date(c.insert_date)) AS rn
  FROM cities c
  WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', c.insert_date) = '2022-06'
),

  SELECT
    country_code,
    inserted_city_date,
    rn,

  FROM RankedDates
),
ConsecutiveStreaks AS (
  SELECT
    country_code,
    grp,
    COUNT(*) AS streak_length
  FROM GroupedDates
  GROUP BY country_code, grp
)
SELECT DISTINCT country_code
FROM ConsecutiveStreaks
WHERE streak_length = (
  SELECT MAX(streak_length) FROM ConsecutiveStreaks
)
ORDER BY country_code;
```

The legislators table uses id_bioguide as the identifier joining with legislators_terms on the same id_bioguide. The state is available in legislators_terms and gender in legislators. Also, terms and their period are defined in legislators_terms by term_start and term_end.

I will write a query to:
- Pick female legislators (gender='F') from legislators.
- Join with legislators_terms on id_bioguide.
- Check for terms that include December 31 by checking if any term's term_start <= December 31 of any year and term_end >= December 31 of that year (we simplify by just looking if term_end date includes '12-31' or possibly term contains dates that include December 31).
- Group by the first state they represented (the earliest term's state).
- Return the state with the highest count of such female legislators.

I will prepare the query accordingly.

  FROM legislators_terms lt
  JOIN FemaleLegislators f ON lt.id_bioguide = f.id_bioguide

  SELECT id_bioguide, state

    SELECT id_bioguide, state, term_start,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id_bioguide ORDER BY term_start) AS rn

), FemaleTermsWithDec31 AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT id_bioguide

  WHERE strftime('%m-%d', term_end) = '12-31'
)
SELECT ffs.state, COUNT(DISTINCT ffs.id_bioguide) AS female_legislators_count
FROM FemaleFirstStates ffs
JOIN FemaleTermsWithDec31 fd ON ffs.id_bioguide = fd.id_bioguide

```sql
WITH StyleScores AS (
  SELECT
    Musical_StyleID,
    SUM(
      CASE PreferenceSeq
        WHEN 1 THEN 3
        WHEN 2 THEN 2
        WHEN 3 THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS TotalWeightedScore

  FROM StyleScores

FROM StyleScores, AverageScore
ORDER BY Musical_StyleID;
```

Given a database of musical styles and user preferences, where Musical_Preferences contains user rankings of musical styles (PreferenceSeq=1 for first choice, PreferenceSeq=2 for second choice, PreferenceSeq=3 for third choice): Calculate a weighted score for each musical style by assigning 3 points for each time it was ranked as first choice, 2 points for each second choice, and 1 point for each third choice ranking. Calculate the total weighted score for each musical style that has been ranked by at least one user. Then, compute the absolute difference between each style's total weighted score and the average total weighted score across all such styles.

```sql
WITH StyleScores AS (
  SELECT
    Musical_StyleID,
    SUM(
      CASE PreferenceSeq
        WHEN 1 THEN 3
        WHEN 2 THEN 2
        WHEN 3 THEN 1
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS TotalWeightedScore
  FROM Musical_Preferences
  WHERE PreferenceSeq IN (1, 2, 3)
  GROUP BY Musical_StyleID
),
AverageScore AS (
  SELECT AVG(TotalWeightedScore) AS AvgScore

)
SELECT
  Musical_StyleID,
  TotalWeightedScore,
  ABS(TotalWeightedScore - AvgScore) AS AbsoluteDifferenceFromAverage
FROM StyleScores, AverageScore
```

```sql
WITH monthly_net AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    STRFTIME('%Y-%m-01', txn_date) AS month_start,
    SUM(CASE WHEN txn_type = 'deposit' THEN txn_amount ELSE -txn_amount END) AS net_amount
  FROM customer_transactions
  GROUP BY customer_id, month_start
),
closing_balance AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    month_start,
    SUM(net_amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS closing_balance
  FROM monthly_net
),
latest_growth AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    month_start,
    closing_balance,
    LAG(closing_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_balance,
    CASE 
      WHEN LAG(closing_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start) = 0 OR LAG(closing_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start) IS NULL
        THEN closing_balance * 100
      ELSE
        (closing_balance - LAG(closing_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start)) * 100.0 / LAG(closing_balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start)
    END AS growth_rate
  FROM closing_balance
),
most_recent_month AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    growth_rate
  FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, growth_rate, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start DESC) AS rank
    FROM latest_growth
  )
  WHERE rank = 1
)
SELECT
  100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN growth_rate > 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS pct_customers_growth_above_5
FROM most_recent_month;
```

```sql
        CAST(m.year AS INTEGER) AS year
    FROM M_Cast c

    GROUP BY PID
```

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE months(month_start) AS (
  SELECT date(min(txn_date), 'start of month')
  FROM customer_transactions
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(month_start, '+1 month')
  FROM months
  WHERE month_start < (SELECT date(max(txn_date), 'start of month') FROM customer_transactions)
),

customer_months AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, month_start
  FROM months CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM customer_transactions)
),

monthly_balances AS (
  SELECT
    cm.customer_id,
    cm.month_start,
    COALESCE(SUM(ct.txn_amount), 0) AS monthly_change
  FROM customer_months cm
  LEFT JOIN customer_transactions ct ON ct.customer_id = cm.customer_id
    AND date(ct.txn_date, 'start of month') = cm.month_start
  GROUP BY cm.customer_id, cm.month_start
),

cumulative_balances AS (
  SELECT 
    customer_id,
    month_start,
    monthly_change,
    SUM(monthly_change) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY month_start ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_balance
  FROM monthly_balances
)

SELECT customer_id, month_start AS month, monthly_change, cumulative_balance
FROM cumulative_balances
ORDER BY customer_id, month_start;
```

```sql
WITH region_year_summaries AS (
  SELECT 
    region,
    STRFTIME('%Y', created_at) AS year,
    SUM(transaction_dollar_amount) AS total_dollar_amount,
    SUM(transaction_btc_amount) AS total_btc_amount,
    MIN(STRFTIME('%Y', created_at)) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS first_year_per_region
  FROM bitcoin_transactions
  GROUP BY region, year
),
filtered_summaries AS (
  SELECT
    region,
    year,
    total_dollar_amount,
    total_btc_amount
  FROM region_year_summaries
  WHERE year > first_year_per_region
),
avg_price_per_year AS (
  SELECT
    region,
    year,
    total_dollar_amount / total_btc_amount AS avg_purchase_price
  FROM filtered_summaries
),
ranked_avg_price AS (
  SELECT
    region,
    year,
    avg_purchase_price,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY avg_purchase_price DESC) AS price_rank
  FROM avg_price_per_year
),
price_changes AS (
  SELECT
    cur.region,
    cur.year,
    cur.avg_purchase_price,
    cur.price_rank,
    CASE 
      WHEN prev.avg_purchase_price IS NULL THEN NULL
      ELSE 100.0 * (cur.avg_purchase_price - prev.avg_purchase_price) / prev.avg_purchase_price
    END AS annual_pct_change
  FROM ranked_avg_price cur
  LEFT JOIN ranked_avg_price prev
    ON cur.region = prev.region
    AND CAST(cur.year AS INTEGER) = CAST(prev.year AS INTEGER) + 1
)
SELECT *
FROM price_changes
ORDER BY year, price_rank;
```

Provided benchmark documentation:
# Special Words Definition

## Batting Average
- Batting average is a measure of a batsman's performance, calculated by dividing the total number of runs scored by the number of times they have been dismissed. A higher batting average indicates a more consistent and successful batsman.
- Batting Average = Total Runs ÷ Total Dismissals

## Strike Rate
- In batting, strike rate indicates the scoring rate of a batsman, showing the average number of runs scored per 100 balls faced. A higher strike rate reflects an aggressive and fast-scoring batsman.
- Strike Rate = (Total Runs ÷ Balls Faced) × 100

## Wickets Taken
- Wickets taken refers to the total number of times a bowler has successfully dismissed an opposing batsman. This statistic is a core measure of a bowler's effectiveness and impact on the game.

## Economy Rate
- Economy rate measures a bowler's efficiency by indicating the average number of runs conceded per over (6 balls) bowled. A lower economy rate shows greater control and efficiency in restricting the opposition's scoring.
- Economy Rate = (Total Runs Conceded ÷ Balls Bowled) × 6

## Wickets Taken
- The number of times a bowler successfully dismisses a batsman in a single match.  This metric is a direct indicator of the bowler's effectiveness, showing how many players they were able to remove from play.

## Runs Given
- The total number of runs scored by the batting side off a particular bowler’s deliveries in a single match.  This value reflects the runs the bowler has conceded to the batting team, and a lower runs-given value is typically favorable for the bowler's performance.

WITH inventory_ordered AS (
  SELECT
    i.product_id,
    i.location_id,
    i.quantity_available,
    MIN(p.purchase_date) AS earliest_purchase_date
  FROM inventory i
  JOIN purchases p ON i.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY i.product_id, i.location_id, i.quantity_available

inventory_ranked AS (
  SELECT

The activity_log table contains a column named "session" for session identifier and a column named "path" for the web page visited. The timestamp column is named "stamp." I will revise the query to use these column names accordingly.

```sql
WITH first_last_per_session AS (
  SELECT
    session,
    MIN(stamp) AS landing_ts,
    MAX(stamp) AS exit_ts
  FROM activity_log
  GROUP BY session
),
landing_pages AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    a.session,
    a.path AS web_page
  FROM activity_log a
  JOIN first_last_per_session s
    ON a.session = s.session AND a.stamp = s.landing_ts
),
exit_pages AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    a.session,
    a.path AS web_page
  FROM activity_log a
  JOIN first_last_per_session s
    ON a.session = s.session AND a.stamp = s.exit_ts
),
combined_pages AS (
  SELECT * FROM landing_pages
  UNION
  SELECT * FROM exit_pages
)
SELECT
  web_page,
  COUNT(DISTINCT session) AS unique_sessions
FROM combined_pages
GROUP BY web_page
ORDER BY unique_sessions DESC;
```

The activity_log table contains a column named "session" for session identifier and a column named "path" for the web page visited. The timestamp column is named "stamp." I will revise the query to use these column names accordingly.

```sql
WITH first_last_per_session AS (
  SELECT
    session,
    MIN(stamp) AS landing_ts,
    MAX(stamp) AS exit_ts
  FROM activity_log
  GROUP BY session
),
landing_pages AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    a.session,
    a.path AS web_page
  FROM activity_log a
  JOIN first_last_per_session s

),
exit_pages AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    a.session,
    a.path AS web_page
  FROM activity_log a
  JOIN first_last_per_session s
    ON a.session = s.session AND a.stamp = s.exit_ts
),
combined_pages AS (
  SELECT * FROM landing_pages
  UNION
  SELECT * FROM exit_pages
)
SELECT
  web_page,
  COUNT(DISTINCT session) AS unique_sessions
FROM combined_pages
GROUP BY web_page
ORDER BY unique_sessions DESC;
```

I will calculate the average number of new unicorn companies per year in the top industry from 2019 to 2021.
- Define unicorn companies as those with valuation >= 1 billion in companies_funding.
- Join with companies_industries to get industry and with companies_dates to get year_founded.
- Filter unicorns founded between 2019 and 2021.
- Group by industry to find the top industry by count.
- Calculate average new unicorns per year in that industry over 2019-2021.

```sql
WITH unicorns AS (
    SELECT f.company_id, i.industry, d.year_founded
    FROM companies_funding f
    JOIN companies_industries i ON f.company_id = i.company_id
    JOIN companies_dates d ON f.company_id = d.company_id
    WHERE f.valuation >= 1000000000
      AND d.year_founded BETWEEN 2019 AND 2021
),
industry_counts AS (
    SELECT industry, COUNT(DISTINCT company_id) AS unicorn_count

top_industry AS (

    ORDER BY unicorn_count DESC
    LIMIT 1
),
unicorns_in_top_industry AS (
    SELECT year_founded, COUNT(DISTINCT company_id) AS new_unicorns
    FROM unicorns
    WHERE industry = (SELECT industry FROM top_industry)
    GROUP BY year_founded
)
SELECT AVG(new_unicorns) AS avg_new_unicorns_per_year
FROM unicorns_in_top_industry;
```

transcript.content:
Based on monthly sales data starting in January 2016 and using a centered moving average to adjust for seasonality, which products had a seasonality-adjusted sales ratio that stayed consistently above 2 for every month in the year 2017?

Provided benchmark documentation:

# Explanation of Metrics

## 1. Sales-to-CMA Ratio
- **Definition**: This ratio compares actual sales to the centered moving average (CMA) of sales.
- **Calculation**:
  - **Centered Moving Average (CMA)**: The CMA is a smoothed value of sales calculated over a rolling 12-month period. It averages sales from the months before and after a given month, specifically using two overlapping windows (5 months before and 6 months after, and vice versa).
  - **Sales-to-CMA Ratio**: The ratio is computed by dividing the actual sales amount for a month by its corresponding CMA value. A ratio greater than 2 indicates that the actual sales are more than twice the smoothed average for that period, suggesting significantly higher-than-average sales.

## 2. 12-Month Overlapping Windows
- **Definition**: A method to smooth sales data over time by averaging values in a specified window.
- **Calculation**:
  - **Window Size**: The window spans 12 months, with the specific approach involving overlapping periods. 
  - **First Window**: For a given month, this window includes 5 months before and 6 months after.
  - **Second Window**: Another window includes 6 months before and 5 months after the given month.
  - **Averaging**: Sales data is averaged over these two overlapping windows to compute the CMA. This method smooths out fluctuations by considering both the past and future sales in the calculation.

## 3. Restriction to the 7th and 30th Months
- **Definition**: A filter applied to focus calculations within a specific range of months.
- **Calculation**:
  - **Time Range**: Only the months between the 7th and 30th time steps (which correspond to specific periods) are considered for calculating the CMA and ratio.
  - **Purpose**: This restriction is used to avoid edge effects in the data where the moving average might be less reliable (e.g., at the very beginning or end of the available data). By focusing on these months, the calculations are more stable and meaningful.

# Flight Route Distance Calculation

## Introduction

This document describes the method used to calculate the distance between two cities for flight routes. The calculation is based on the Haversine formula, which is commonly used to find the shortest distance between two points on a sphere given their latitude and longitude. This method is especially useful for determining flight distances between airports located in different cities around the world.

## City and Coordinate Extraction

For each flight, the following data is obtained:

- **Departure city** (referred to as `from_city`) and its geographical coordinates (longitude and latitude).
- **Arrival city** (referred to as `to_city`) and its geographical coordinates (longitude and latitude).

The coordinates are extracted as decimal values, with longitude and latitude represented in degrees. This ensures that trigonometric operations can be applied during the distance calculation.

## Haversine Formula

The Haversine formula is used to calculate the great-circle distance between two points on a sphere using their latitude and longitude. The formula is given as:

\[
d = 2r \cdot \arcsin\left(\sqrt{\sin^2\left(\frac{\Delta \phi}{2}\right) + \cos(\phi_1) \cdot \cos(\phi_2) \cdot \sin^2\left(\frac{\Delta \lambda}{2}\right)}\right)
\]

Where:

- \( d \) is the distance between the two points (in kilometers).
- \( r \) is the radius of the Earth (approximately 6371 km).
- \( \phi_1 \) and \( \phi_2 \) are the latitudes of the departure and arrival points, respectively, in radians.
- \( \Delta \phi = \phi_2 - \phi_1 \) is the difference in latitudes.
- \( \lambda_1 \) and \( \lambda_2 \) are the longitudes of the departure and arrival points, respectively, in radians.
- \( \Delta \lambda = \lambda_2 - \lambda_1 \) is the difference in longitudes.

### Conversion to Radians

Since the input coordinates are in degrees, they must be converted to radians before applying the Haversine formula. This conversion is done using the formula:

\[
\text{radians} = \text{degrees} \times \frac{\pi}{180}
\]

## Symmetry of Routes

To identify unique flight routes between two cities, we standardize the order of cities in each route. Specifically, we ensure that the lexicographically smaller city name is always listed as the first city (`city1`), and the larger city is listed as the second city (`city2`). This ensures that a flight from City A to City B is treated the same as a flight from City B to City A.

## Average Route Distance

Once the distances for all flights between two cities are computed, the average distance for each city pair is calculated by summing the distances and dividing by the total number of flights between those cities:

\[
\text{Average Distance} = \frac{\sum \text{Flight Distances}}{\text{Number of Flights}}
\]

## Conclusion

This method of flight route distance calculation provides a reliable way to determine the great-circle distance between cities based on the coordinates of their respective airports. The use of the Haversine formula ensures accurate results for distances on the Earth's surface, making it ideal for aviation and travel analysis.

    )) AS distance_km
  FROM city_pairs
),

avg_distances AS (
  SELECT
    city1,
    city2,
    AVG(distance_km) AS avg_distance
  FROM haversine_distances
  GROUP BY city1, city2
),

ranges AS (
  SELECT
    city1,
    city2,
    avg_distance,
    CASE
      WHEN avg_distance < 1000 THEN 0
      WHEN avg_distance < 2000 THEN 1000
      WHEN avg_distance < 3000 THEN 2000
      WHEN avg_distance < 4000 THEN 3000
      WHEN avg_distance < 5000 THEN 4000
      WHEN avg_distance < 6000 THEN 5000
      ELSE 6000
    END AS distance_range
  FROM avg_distances
),

count_by_range AS (
  SELECT distance_range, COUNT(*) AS pairs_count
  FROM ranges
  GROUP BY distance_range
),

least_range AS (
  SELECT distance_range, pairs_count
  FROM count_by_range
  ORDER BY pairs_count ASC
  LIMIT 1
)

SELECT pairs_count
FROM least_range;

In the results table, the correct column names are driver_id and constructor_id. In the races table, the year column for seasons is called year. Using these corrected column names, I will run the query to identify the top five constructors with the most seasons since 2001 where their drivers scored the fewest total points among all drivers who scored points in that season. I will consider only drivers who scored points in a season, so total_points > 0 must be ensured.

```sql
WITH season_driver_points AS (
  SELECT 
    ra.year AS season,
    r.driver_id,
    r.constructor_id,
    SUM(r.points) AS total_points
  FROM results r
  JOIN races ra ON r.race_id = ra.race_id
  WHERE ra.year >= 2001
  GROUP BY ra.year, r.driver_id, r.constructor_id
  HAVING total_points > 0
),
season_min_points AS (
  SELECT 
    season,
    MIN(total_points) AS min_points
  FROM season_driver_points
  GROUP BY season
),
season_driver_min AS (
  SELECT sdp.season, sdp.driver_id, sdp.constructor_id, sdp.total_points
  FROM season_driver_points sdp
  JOIN season_min_points smp ON sdp.season = smp.season AND sdp.total_points = smp.min_points
),
season_min_constructor AS (
  SELECT 
    season,
    constructor_id
  FROM season_driver_min
  GROUP BY season, constructor_id
),
constructor_min_seasons_count AS (
  SELECT 
    constructor_id,
    COUNT(season) AS min_seasons_count
  FROM season_min_constructor
  GROUP BY constructor_id
)

FROM constructor_min_seasons_count cmsc
JOIN constructors c ON cmsc.constructor_id = c.constructor_id
ORDER BY cmsc.min_seasons_count DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Considering all races where pit stop data is available, and focusing on instances when a driver was not behind another car on the previous lap but is behind on the current lap (accounting for retirements, pit-stop entries, pit-stop exits, and race starts), how many times has each type of overtake occurred in Formula 1?

Provided benchmark documentation:
# Overtake Label Classification

In racing, overtakes are categorized into different states based on specific conditions, reflecting the circumstances in which the overtaking occurred. Below are the classifications and their detailed explanations:

## 1. R (Retirement) - Overtake during Retirement
An overtake is labeled as **R (Retirement)** if the overtaken driver retired on the same lap as the overtake. This indicates that the overtake occurred just before or during the overtaken driver's retirement, meaning they could no longer continue the race after that lap.

## 2. P (Pit) - Overtake related to Pit Stops
An overtake is classified as **P (Pit)** under two scenarios:
   - **Pit Entry**: If the overtake occurred while the overtaken driver was entering the pit lane, and the driver pitted on the same lap, it indicates that the overtaking happened due to the overtaken driver reducing speed to enter the pit lane.
   - **Pit Exit**: If the overtake occurred as the overtaken driver was exiting the pit lane, especially if the driver pitted on the previous lap and the time gap between the drivers was less than a typical pit stop duration. This suggests that the overtake happened while the overtaken driver was potentially at a lower speed, rejoining the race track from the pit lane.

## 3. S (Start) - Overtake at Race Start
If the overtake took place on the first lap of the race, and the two drivers were within two grid positions of each other at the start, the overtake is classified as **S (Start)**. This classification indicates that the overtake was part of the initial racing shuffle during the race's launch phase, where close position changes are common.

## 4. T (Track) - Overtake under Normal Racing Conditions
If none of the above conditions apply, the overtake is categorized as **T (Track)**, meaning it occurred during normal racing conditions on the track, without any external factors like pit stops or retirements influencing the outcome. This is the default classification for overtakes that happen during regular competition.

---

These classifications help to identify and record the context of each overtake with clarity, ensuring accurate representation of race dynamics.

WITH pit_lap_numbers AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT race_id, driver_id, lap
    FROM pit_stops
),

-- Identify overtakes where a driver was not behind another driver in previous lap but is behind in current lap
overtakes AS (
    SELECT
        curr.race_id,
        curr.lap,
        curr.driver_id AS overtaking_driver_id,
        curr.behind_driver_id AS overtaken_driver_id
    FROM (
        SELECT
            curr.lap_positions.race_id,
            curr.lap_positions.lap,
            curr.lap_positions.driver_id,
            prev.lap_positions.driver_id AS behind_driver_id
        FROM lap_positions curr
        LEFT JOIN lap_positions prev ON
            curr.race_id = prev.race_id AND
            curr.lap = prev.lap + 1 AND
            curr.driver_id = prev.driver_id
        WHERE curr.behind_driver_id IS NOT NULL
    ) curr
    LEFT JOIN (
        SELECT
            prev.lap_positions.race_id,
            prev.lap_positions.lap + 1 AS lap,
            prev.lap_positions.driver_id,
            prev.lap_positions.behind_driver_id
        FROM lap_positions prev
    ) prev ON
        curr.race_id = prev.race_id AND
        curr.lap = prev.lap AND
        curr.driver_id = prev.driver_id AND
        curr.behind_driver_id = prev.behind_driver_id
    WHERE prev.behind_driver_id IS NULL
),

-- Join pit_stop info, retirements, race starts, and determine type of overtake
classified_overtakes AS (
    SELECT
        o.race_id,
        o.lap,
        o.overtaking_driver_id,
        o.overtaken_driver_id,
        -- Check retirement: overtaken driver retired on this lap
        CASE WHEN r.driver_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'R'
             -- Check pit entry: overtaken driver pitting this lap and slowed down
             WHEN pit_entry.lap IS NOT NULL THEN 'P'
             -- Check pit exit: overtaken driver pitted previous lap and time gap small
             WHEN pit_exit.lap IS NOT NULL THEN 'P'
             -- Check start: lap 1 and positions within 2 on grid
             WHEN s.position IS NOT NULL THEN 'S'
             ELSE 'T' END AS overtake_type
    FROM overtakes o
    LEFT JOIN retirements r ON r.race_id = o.race_id AND r.driver_id = o.overtaken_driver_id AND r.lap = o.lap
    LEFT JOIN (
        SELECT race_id, driver_id, lap FROM pit_stops
    ) pit_entry ON pit_entry.race_id = o.race_id AND pit_entry.driver_id = o.overtaken_driver_id AND pit_entry.lap = o.lap
    LEFT JOIN (
        SELECT ps.race_id, ps.driver_id, ps.lap
        FROM pit_stops ps
        JOIN races r ON r.race_id = ps.race_id
        WHERE EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 FROM pit_stops ps2 WHERE ps2.race_id = ps.race_id AND ps2.driver_id = ps.driver_id AND ps2.lap = ps.lap - 1
        )
    ) pit_exit ON pit_exit.race_id = o.race_id AND pit_exit.driver_id = o.overtaken_driver_id AND pit_exit.lap = o.lap
    LEFT JOIN (
        SELECT race_id, driver_id, grid_position AS position
        FROM qualifying
        WHERE race_id IN (SELECT DISTINCT race_id FROM pit_stops)
    ) s ON s.race_id = o.race_id AND s.driver_id IN (o.overtaking_driver_id, o.overtaken_driver_id)
    WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM qualifying
        WHERE race_id = o.race_id
        AND ((driver_id = o.overtaking_driver_id AND grid_position IS NOT NULL) OR (driver_id = o.overtaken_driver_id AND grid_position IS NOT NULL))
    )
),

-- Aggregate counts by overtake type
result AS (
    SELECT overtake_type, COUNT(*) AS occurences
    FROM classified_overtakes
    GROUP BY overtake_type
)

SELECT * FROM result;

```sql
  FROM driver_standings ds

  FROM constructor_standings cs

combined_points AS (

    cst.constructor_points,
    d.max_points_per_driver + cst.constructor_points AS total_points
  FROM driver_points d

  JOIN constructors c
    ON d.constructorId = c.constructorId
),
ranked_points AS (
  SELECT
    season,
    constructorId,
    constructor_name,
    total_points,

  FROM combined_points

  SELECT
```

```sql
WITH driver_points AS (
  SELECT
    ds.driverId,
    ds.season,
    ds.constructorId,
    MAX(ds.points) AS max_points_per_driver
  FROM driver_standings ds
  GROUP BY ds.driverId, ds.season, ds.constructorId
),

    cs.season,
    cs.points AS constructor_points
  FROM constructor_standings cs
),
combined_points AS (
  SELECT
    d.season,
    d.constructorId,
    c.name AS constructor_name,
    d.driverId,
    d.max_points_per_driver,
    cst.constructor_points,
    d.max_points_per_driver + cst.constructor_points AS total_points
  FROM driver_points d
  JOIN constructor_points cst
    ON d.constructorId = cst.constructorId AND d.season = cst.season
  JOIN constructors c
    ON d.constructorId = c.constructorId
),
ranked_points AS (
  SELECT
    season,
    constructorId,
    constructor_name,
    total_points,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY season ORDER BY total_points DESC) AS rank_in_season
  FROM combined_points
)
SELECT
  constructor_name,
  season,
  total_points
FROM (
  SELECT
    constructor_name,
    season,
    total_points,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_points DESC) AS rank_overall
  FROM ranked_points
  WHERE rank_in_season = 1
)
WHERE rank_overall <= 3
ORDER BY rank_overall;
```

```sql
WITH over_runs AS (
  SELECT
    m.match_id,
    b.inning,
    b.over,
    SUM(bs.runs) AS batsman_runs,
    COALESCE(SUM(e.extra_runs), 0) AS extra_runs
  FROM
    match m
    JOIN ball_by_ball b ON m.match_id = b.match_id
    LEFT JOIN batsman_scored bs ON b.match_id = bs.match_id AND b.inning = bs.inning AND b.over = bs.over AND b.ball = bs.ball
    LEFT JOIN extra_runs e ON b.match_id = e.match_id AND b.inning = e.inning AND b.over = e.over AND b.ball = e.ball
  GROUP BY
    m.match_id,
    b.inning,
    b.over
),
over_with_bowler AS (
  SELECT
    o.match_id,
    o.inning,
    o.over,
    o.batsman_runs + o.extra_runs AS total_runs,
    bb.bowler
  FROM
    over_runs o
    JOIN (
      SELECT DISTINCT
        match_id,
        inning,
        over,
        bowler
      FROM
        ball_by_ball
    ) bb ON o.match_id = bb.match_id AND o.inning = bb.inning AND o.over = bb.over
),
max_over_per_match_inning AS (
  SELECT
    match_id,
    inning,
    total_runs,
    bowler
  FROM (
    SELECT
      match_id,
      inning,
      total_runs,
      bowler,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY match_id, inning ORDER BY total_runs DESC, bowler) AS rn
    FROM
      over_with_bowler
  )
  WHERE rn = 1
),
max_over_per_match AS (
  SELECT
    match_id,
    total_runs,
    bowler
  FROM (
    SELECT
      match_id,
      total_runs,
      bowler,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY match_id ORDER BY total_runs DESC) AS rn
    FROM
      max_over_per_match_inning
  )
  WHERE rn = 1
)
SELECT
  AVG(total_runs) AS average_highest_over_total_runs
FROM
  max_over_per_match;
```
